doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Writing obituaries for The Guardian
summary: He writes Guardian obituaries, sometimes in advance, and keeps files on key musicians; he recalls the Kenny Baker deadline.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah. I understand that you also have a role sometimes that you don’t really enjoy and that’s writing obituaries for people that are still with us?

Yeah. Well I’m an obituary writer for “The Guardian” which is a national newspaper. And as often the case, one is writing obituaries ahead of time. It’s a peculiar feeling. I also find it creatively quite hard to do because somehow, you know if I ring the paper, I mean do you remember Kenny Baker, the British trumpet player?

Well I got the first news of his death and I phoned the paper and they said fine. It was like this was four o’clock in the afternoon. And they said can you have 800 words by six o’clock, which concentrates the mind, doesn’t it? And somehow the adrenaline gets that going. It really works. I’m a deadline person. If someone said let’s have it done by six o’clock you think get cracking. I’ll just leave that let’s go. And somehow the adrenaline for that is different to that that’s required for this obituary that one is doing ahead of time. Do you understand me?
But you’ve got to have a great deal of knowledge already to sort of do that. You can’t start saying where’s the book, you know, and start from scratch.

The guys I write about, who the paper would expect me to be able to write about, I’ve usually got a file on them. I’ve got extensive files on key individuals. Because I mean I’m interested. I’m just a magpie for information. So I’ve got a whole house full of stuff. Talk to my wife and she’ll tell you that the piles are getting bigger.
